title: Buyers, sellers, and the people forgiving the debt
body:
## The buyers: carving up a century

Unitika's restructuring is not a single transaction. It is a slow disaggregation of a conglomerate assembled across four decades of post-war diversification, and understanding what it reveals requires knowing not just what Unitika is selling — but who is willing to buy, and at what price.

The clearest completed transaction is Zuiko Corporation's 2025 acquisition of Unitika's spunlace cotton nonwovens operation, marketed under the COTEX brand. [Zuiko (6279.T)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/zuiko-corporation_cotton-spunlace-nonwovens-activity-7343573455486783489-r33y), an Osaka-based maker of nonwovens converting machinery, was a logical acquirer — the business is adjacent to its equipment lines. That it closed at all is notable: Unitika's fibers-and-textiles segment posted only ¥50 million in operating profit on ¥23.9 billion in revenue through the nine months to December 2025, a margin thin enough to suggest buyers are negotiating hard.

More complex is the Okazaki textile transaction, where [Seiren Co. (3569.T)](https://www.tipranks.com/news/company-announcements/seiren-co-to-acquire-new-textile-business-from-unitika-and-nippon-ester) is acquiring the textile operations at Unitika's Okazaki plant — a business carved jointly from Unitika and its affiliate Nippon Ester Co. The structure requires first separating the assets into a newly formed entity, then transferring ownership, a sequence that leaves closing risk latent. Seiren brings a credible rationale: it has spent the past decade building a high-function textiles business and sees legacy capacity as raw material for product repositioning. Whether it paid fair value cannot be confirmed from public disclosures.

One asset remains conspicuously unsold. TUSCO, the Thailand-based polyester spunbond operation, was [still seeking a buyer as of October 2025](https://www.nonwovens-industry.com/breaking-news/unitika-seeking-buyer-for-nonwovens-business/). Polyester spunbond is a competitive commodity; Southeast Asian capacity is abundant and margins are thin. The longer TUSCO sits on the block, the more it constrains Unitika's narrative of orderly exit.

## The partner that legitimises the pivot

If the divestitures tell you what Unitika is abandoning, the December 2025 announcement with DIC Corporation tells you what it wants to be taken seriously for. At CES 2026, DIC and Unitika announced co-development of polyphenylene sulfide (PPS) film for millimetre-wave printed circuit boards and automotive radar substrates — material that must survive 100 GHz signals with minimal dielectric loss, and that tolerates the thermal cycles inherent in engine-bay deployment.

The partnership is structurally asymmetric in Unitika's favour in one important sense: DIC (4631.T) is a ¥900 billion-revenue specialty chemicals conglomerate — roughly eight times Unitika's current guided revenue of ¥110 billion. When a company that size chooses a co-development partner for a strategic mmWave material, it is implicitly validating that partner's process know-how. Unitika's PPS film capability, developed within its high-polymer segment, had previously generated operating profit of ¥7.5 billion through the nine-month period — 67% above the prior year — driven partly by industrial film demand. The DIC partnership is the bet that this capability can be repositioned from commodity industrial to high-specification electronic, where pricing power is structurally different.

The caveat is timing. Automotive radar volumes grow on vehicle-electrification timelines; mmWave PCB penetration depends on infrastructure buildout. Neither is certain enough to call the DIC partnership commercially proven. It is a credible option, not a contracted revenue stream.

## Customers hiding in the segment commentary

Unitika's investor disclosures do not publish customer concentration figures, but the segment commentary from the nine months to December 2025 is revealing when read carefully. Food-packaging end users drove strong demand for the EMBLEM-HG high-barrier nylon film — a domestic Japan story tied to convenience food growth. Semiconductor substrate manufacturers adopted UniPeel, Unitika's silicone-free release film, for capacitor and substrate processing. And mobile memory manufacturers — specifically those supplying high-end smartphones — were called out as buyers of the ultra-thin Low CTE and E Glass Fabrics from the performance-materials segment, where operating profit tripled year-on-year to ¥1.4 billion.

These are not glamorous end markets in the venture-capital sense, but they share a property: the customer cannot easily qualify a substitute once a film or fabric is embedded in a process. Qualification cycles in semiconductor manufacturing run twelve to eighteen months. That stickiness, if it holds, is worth more than any single contract value.

## The banks, the backstop, and the exit clock

Underneath the asset sales and partnership announcements sits an act of institutional forbearance that is unusual even by Japanese standards. MUFG, Mizuho, and Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Bank collectively forgave up to ¥43 billion in Unitika debt — a number that exceeds three times the company's FY3/25 shareholders' equity of ¥15.6 billion. The mechanism that made this possible is the Regional Economic Vitalization Corporation of Japan (REVIC), a government-affiliated revitalization fund that orchestrated the restructuring, injected ¥20 billion via a third-party Class C preferred share allotment completed on 30 April 2025, and extended a separate ¥15 billion financing line.

The effect on the balance sheet was immediate and dramatic. Capital adequacy rose from 10.4% at the FY3/25 year-end to 25.2% through the nine months to December 2025. Cash and deposits jumped from ¥13.5 billion to ¥57.9 billion — a ¥44.5 billion increase driven by the REVIC injection and asset-sale proceeds.

Why do Japanese main banks agree to terms like this? The answer is structural, not altruistic. Lender concentration in Japanese corporate finance means a handful of banks hold the majority of a company's debt; they have no liquid secondary market to exit into and no US-style Chapter 11 to force rapid liquidation. Walking away means absorbing a loss and triggering a cascade that damages related credits. REVIC's presence — which carries implicit government backing and a formal restructuring mandate — provides cover for the banks to reclassify forgiven debt as part of an orchestrated recovery rather than a unilateral write-down.

That restructuring mandate is the detail Unitika's common shareholders should hold in mind. REVIC holds 66.76% of votes through its Class C preferred shares. Its institutional mission is to fix distressed companies and exit — not to compound indefinitely. The ¥2.27 per share Class C dividend forecast for FY3/26 is modest; the real return to REVIC will come from eventual disposal of its stake, whether through a trade sale, secondary offering, or managed wind-down of the preferred position. The clock is running. How fast it runs depends on whether the FY3/29 target — ¥70 billion in revenue at 9.3% operating margin — begins to look achievable in the interim results.
